Follow live updates here. Budgeting For Growth In A Time Of Inflation
 London Business School, Contributor Wed, October 28, 2026 at 11:45 AM MST 5 min read How does a government budget for growth during record inflation? Economist Linda Yueh breaks down the UK's latest fiscal strategy and its tight constraints. By Dr Linda Yueh CBE, Adjunct Professor of Economics at the London Business School 
 The first Budget of the British Chancellor John Healey showed the challenge of budgeting under inflationary pressures whilst simultaneously signalling a growth strategy to achieve growth "in every postcode." This aspiration reflects the devolution aims of the new Prime Minister Andy Burnham, some of which was evident in the Budget with 20 per cent of business rates going to mayoral authorities from next year and a share of tax receipts from 2028 going to local authorities. 
 But, unsurprisingly, the central issue was the cost of living. Inflation is expected to reach 3.7 per cent in early 2027 and not expected to return to the Bank of England's two per cent target until the end of next year. The resultant cost of living pressure has contributed to an "extraordinary collapse" in consumer confidence and struggling retail sales. Accordingly, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) believes that the economy will grow at just one per cent down from 1.6% next year. 
 The Budget thus funded measures to reduce energy bills for households, among others, to support disposable income. But current spending needs to be covered by tax revenues in order to meet the government's fiscal rule. So, rather than stimulate growth, the spending is to help people and the economy tread water by offsetting some of the pressures on households and businesses. 
 The other source of pressure on the Chancellor's "fiscal headroom," which is the difference between expected spending and tax revenues, is from the direct impact on government debt from inflation. The fiscal space has shrunk to £15bn from just under £24bn but will recover by 2030-2031. Among the reasons are debt interest payments, which have increased on inflation-linked gilts that account for about a quarter of the UK's debt. Indeed, the Chancellor said previously that if debt interest was a government department, it would be the second largest spending category at over £109bn per annum. 
 Also, due to inflation, the Bank of England is holding interest rates at 3.75 per cent and borrowing costs are likely to stay higher for longer. The U.S. and Japan have already raised rates, so the UK may well follow suit if global inflationary pressures remain elevated. The OBR believes it will and expects rates to rise to around 4.25 per cent by mid-2027. That would only worsen the pressure on the fiscal headroom, which could lead to more tax rises to cover debt payments, which would dampen economic growth. Lower economic growth would lead to lower tax receipts, so that's why it's particularly challenging to grow during a time of significant inflationary pressures. 
 Story Continues It's also challenging to raise taxes when income tax, VAT, and National Insurance can't be increased due to the Labour Party Manifesto. So, the tax burden is spread on smaller tax sources. Thus, increasing the bank levy and closing a loophole on VAT on goods sold on online marketplaces are among the measures announced in the Budget. Indeed, there are 98 measures included in the Treasury scorecard, most either cost or raise less than £1bn. 
 Also, the tax take has traditionally been below 40 per cent of GDP while public spending has been for many years above 40 per cent of GDP. Departmental spending on the NHS and education as well as welfare and pensions are among the largest categories, but also some of the areas that face the strongest pressures due to health and pensions costs rising with an ageing population. As the tax take is structurally below spending, cutting spending would be needed unless taxes can be reformed and even potentially increased if it is simplified. The UK is close to the OECD average in terms of tax take but is one of the most complicated with cliff edges where rates change dramatically and distort behaviour, so there is scope for improvement. 
 Finally, government debt is a considerable £3trn. Bond investors are already watching debt levels warily so having a structural budget deficit that adds to this debt isn't going to help bring borrowing costs down for either the government or households and businesses. Higher mortgages and cost of capital would indeed inhibit economic growth. It would also raise the cost of the government borrowing to invest, which is a separate fiscal rule that seems particularly important so given the slow growth rate. The capital allocations announced for "dual use" defence technologies, meaning the technology has civilian use and can boost economic growth, is an example of reassuring bond investor that there will be a financial return in the future. 
 Under different circumstances perhaps this Budget could have shown more of how fiscal policy would support growth everywhere across the UK. But, this was perhaps a Budget for its time. 
 Dr Linda Yueh CBE FREcon is an accomplished economist, academic, author, and broadcaster. An Adjunct Professor at London Business School, Dr Yueh serves as Fellow in Economics at St Edmund Hall, Oxford as well as Associate Fellow at Chatham House. Appointed CBE in 2023 for services to economics, she is a Founding Fellow of the Royal Economic Society and a Fellow of the Royal Society of Arts. She holds numerous leadership and advisory roles, including Chair of The Royal Parks, Non-Executive Director of FTSE 100 companies such as Rentokil Initial, SEGRO, and Standard Chartered, Chair of Baillie Gifford's The Schiehallion Fund, trustee of the Fidelity UK and International Foundations, and member of advisory boards at LSE IDEAS and the Centre for Economic Performance. Dr Yueh is a prolific author of 11 books, including The Great Crashes and The Great Economists , and serves as Editor of the Routledge Economic Growth and Development series. Dr Yueh was recently appointed a Non Executive Director of the Independent Football Regulator , following her selection by the Department for Culture, Media and Sport .
